 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
        Aaron Edward Howton, appearing pro se as Intervenor Party No. 250, files this Initial
Post-Hearing Brief opposing the certification of any route that includes Link F-20 and
respectfully submits the following.

                                I. TABLE OF AUTHORITIES
A. Tex. Util. Code § 37.057
B. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c)(4)
C. Tex. Util. Code § 37.156
D. 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101, including § 25.101(b)(3)(B)
E. 16 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 22.71-.72
F. SOAH Order No. 6, PUC Interchange Item No. 788 (Apr. 20, 2026)

                                  II. STATEMENT OF CASE
        This proceeding arises from H.B. No. 5066 and an application filed by Oncor Electric
Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation ("Applicants") to amend
their respective Certificates of Convenience and Necessity ("CCN") under the Public Utility
Regulatory Act and the rules of the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission"). The
application seeks Commission approval to construct, own, and operate a proposed 765-kilovolt
("kV") electric transmission line and associated facilities in Texas. The 180-day decision
deadline is governed by Tex. Util. Code § 37.057. (SOAH Order No. 6 at 7, PUC Interchange
Item No. 788.) This time constraint imposed an unreasonable burden and asymmetry of input on
landowners who had no knowledge they were going to be affected by this project and its process
until April 2026.
The late addition and notice of Link F-20 materially prejudiced affected landowners because
they were not given the same meaningful opportunity to investigate the route, gather exhibits,
retain help, prepare testimony, and challenge the route as landowners who were notified much
earlier in the process.

       Oncor’s proposed project is designed to extend high-voltage transmission infrastructure
between the Bell County East Switch and the Big Hill Substation, traversing portions of fifteen
counties, including Bell County. The application includes multiple alternative routes and route
segments, including routes incorporating Link F-20 and Link F-21.
        Oncor filed its application on or about March 26, 2026, and the Commission assigned
Docket No. 59475. SOAH Order No. 6 set April 27, 2026 as the intervention deadline and May
13, 2026 as the deadline for intervenor testimony or statements of position. (SOAH Order No. 6
at 4-5, PUC Interchange Item No. 788.) Landowners affected by alternate route changes began
receiving notification packets in the mail on or about April 1, 2026, postmarked March 26, 2026.
Following notice to affected landowners and interested parties, multiple individuals and entities
filed timely motions to intervene. The Commission subsequently referred the matter to SOAH
for a contested-case proceeding.


                                             Page 3
        A prehearing conference was held on June 5, 2026, at which procedural matters,
including the admission of parties and evidentiary matters, were addressed. (Prehearing
Conference Tr. Vol. 1 at 1:1-25, 94:1-95:24.) The case proceeded through discovery, prefiled
testimony, and evidentiary submissions. The hearing on the merits was conducted June 8-12,
2026, during which the Administrative Law Judges received testimony, exhibits, and argument
from the Applicants, Commission Staff, and intervening parties. (SOAH Order No. 6 at 7-8,
PUC Interchange Item No. 788; Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 1:1-24.)
        The proposed transmission line would be constructed as a 765-kV facility within a right-
of-way of approximately 200 feet. The application evaluates multiple routing alternatives based
on engineering constraints, environmental considerations, land use, and other routing factors
identified under applicable law and Commission rules.
         The issues presented in this proceeding include whether the proposed transmission
facilities are necessary to serve the public convenience and necessity and, if so, which proposed
route best satisfies the criteria set forth in PURA and Commission rules. These criteria include,
among other factors, the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional service, the effect
of granting the certificate on the recipient and on any electric utility serving the proximate area,
and routing considerations applicable to transmission lines, including impacts on landowners,
environmental integrity, and community values. Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a), (c)(4); 16 Tex.
Admin. Code § 25.101.
        The parties seek differing relief in this proceeding. Applicants request that the
Commission grant the CCN and approve one of the proposed routes. Intervening parties,
including affected landowners, request that the Commission either deny the application or seek a
legislative extension to the 180-day deadline so affected landowners on alternate routes can
receive the same opportunity to voice their concerns as those landowners who were notified at
the June 25, 2025 public meeting.

                                   III. ISSUES PRESENTED
1. Need for the Proposed Transmission Lines

Whether Applicants demonstrated that the proposed 765-kV transmission line is necessary to
serve the public convenience and necessity, consistent with the requirements of the Public Utility
Regulatory Act.

2. Selection of the Appropriate Route

If the Commission determines that the proposed transmission line is necessary, which alternative
route best satisfies the routing criteria established by statute and Commission rules.

3. Impact on Affected Landowners

Whether the routing analysis and process adequately considered and minimized adverse impacts
on affected landowners, including the number of habitable structures affected and the proximity
of the transmission line to residences.

4. Disproportionate Burden on Individual Landowners

                                              Page 4
 Whether route alternatives incorporating Link F-20 impose a disproportionate burden when
compared with Link F-21 and other available alternatives, and how such disparities should be
weighed in route selection.

5. Failure of Proof Regarding Link F-20

Whether Applicants provided a clear, objective, and persuasive explanation for adding Link F-20
and selecting it over Link F-21 or other less harmful alternatives, and whether the absence of
such explanation weighs against approval of any route using Link F-20.

6. Late Addition and Unequal Preparation Time

Whether the late addition and notice of Link F-20 unfairly prejudiced affected landowners by
denying them the same meaningful opportunity to prepare as landowners on earlier-proposed
routes.

7. Community Values and Existing Land Uses

How the proposed routes affect community values, including established rural residential use,
agricultural operations, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, tornado recovery, and long-standing
land-use patterns in the affected area.

8. Environmental and Cultural Resource Considerations

Whether the routing analysis adequately identified and evaluated environmental impacts and
cultural resources, including endangered-species habitat, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church,
Buttermilk Creek, and archaeological concerns.

9. Reasonable Mitigation and Alternative Selection

Whether reasonable alternative routes exist, including Preferred Route 296, Route 899, Route
499, or another non-F-20 route, that would reduce impacts without materially impairing the
project.




                                             Page 5
                                IV. SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The evidentiary record does not support approval of Applicants’ preferred routing to the extent it
incorporates Link F-20. The most important record problem is that Applicants did not verify
their routing assumptions through a meaningful field survey before proposing and evaluating
Link F-20 and Link F-21 as alternate routes. Applicants relied heavily on desktop mapping,
aerial review, and agency database information, but the record shows that this approach was
incomplete. Because Applicants did not conduct adequate ground verification, they missed at
least one habitable structure on Link F-20, failed to properly identify First Cedar Valley Baptist
Church as a historical and cultural resource, did not conduct F-20-specific endangered-species
field verification before route selection, and did not adequately consider the archaeological
sensitivity of the Buttermilk Creek drainage area. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 174:1-25, 197:9-20;
Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-54:8, 56:1-57:3.)

These omissions are not minor clerical errors. They go directly to the statutory routing factors the
Commission must consider under PURA § 37.056(c)(4), including community values, historical
and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, prudent avoidance, and direct landowner impacts.
Applicants’ Environmental Assessment materials understated the residential impact of Link F-20
by failing to include a habitable structure near First Cedar Valley Baptist Church on Tract 5649.
With that correction, Link F-20 has at least three habitable structures within 500 feet, compared
with only one listed habitable structure within 500 feet on Link F-21. A route recommendation
based on an understated count of homes should not be treated as reliable when a reasonable
alternative link reduces those direct human impacts. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21; Appendix
F, Table 7-5; 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B).)

Applicants also failed to identify First Cedar Valley Baptist Church as both a historical site and a
cultural site for the Cedar Valley community. The church was established in 1942 and has served
the community for more than 80 years. It is not merely a building on a map. It is a place of
worship, funerals, weddings, community gatherings, youth programs, senior events, holiday
events, and community support. It was also a focal point for recovery after the April 12, 2022


                                              Page 6
 tornado. Placing a 765-kV transmission line near this community church on Link F-20 would
create a permanent visual and aesthetic burden and would diminish community values in a way
Applicants did not fairly evaluate. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 115:15-119:8; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at
54:24-55:3; First Cedar Valley Baptist Church Direct Testimony at 1-7, PUC Interchange Item
No. 3995.)

Applicants further admitted that no site-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat field survey
was conducted on Link F-20, that the zero-acre ESA figure relied on a GIS overlay rather than a
field survey, and that field environmental surveys would occur after the Commission selects a
route. The record does not show an F-20-specific USFWS validation comparable to the USFWS
involvement that led Applicants to remove another link. As a result, Applicants did not
adequately evaluate Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat identified on or near Mr. Howton’s
property, did not verify endangered-species concerns with the federal agency responsible for
those issues before proposing Link F-20, and did not fully consider environmental integrity
before proposing Link F-20. Likewise, without meaningful field investigation and local
verification, Applicants did not adequately consider the archaeological sensitivity of the
Buttermilk Creek drainage area when they proposed Link F-20 and Link F-21 as alternate routes.
(Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8, 56:1-57:3; Aaron Edward Howton Exs. 12-15.)

The record also shows that Applicants did not adequately consider the adverse effects of placing
this massive infrastructure near a community still recovering from the April 12, 2022 tornado. A
community that has undergone tornado destruction may remain in recovery for years. The Cedar
Valley area, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, and surrounding landowners should not be
burdened with avoidable additional infrastructure impacts when reasonable alternatives exist.
This is precisely the type of community-value and prudent-avoidance concern the routing factors
are intended to address. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-55:23; Aaron Edward Howton Exs. 10-11.)

Applicants’ testimony and cross-examination responses did not provide a clear, objective, or
persuasive explanation for why Link F-20 was selected over Link F-21 or other available
alternatives. Their inability or unwillingness to identify a reliable factual basis for Link F-20
should weigh heavily against approval of any route using that link. The late addition of Link F-
20 also materially prejudiced affected landowners because they were not given the same
meaningful opportunity to investigate, prepare, and respond as landowners on earlier-proposed
routes. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8; SOAH Order No. 6 at 4-7, PUC Interchange Item
No. 788.)

Changing Route 894 to Route 899, or Route 487 to Route 499, affects only one link and does not
materially compromise route cost, length, engineering requirements, constructability, or
electrical performance. Instead, replacing Link F-20 with Link F-21 would better satisfy PURA §
37.056(c)(4), including community values, prudent avoidance, environmental integrity, historical
and aesthetic values, and direct landowner impacts. PUC Staff witness John Poole ranked Route
296 above Applicants Route 894 (Hearing Tr. Vol 4 at 92:4). Mr. Howton therefore requests that

                                             Page 7
 the Administrative Law Judges recommend Preferred Route 296, Route 899, Route 499, or
another route that avoids Link F-20. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-
207:10.)

                                        V. ARGUMENT
A. Introduction
        Intervenor Aaron Edward Howton respectfully submits this Initial Post-Hearing Brief as
an affected landowner and pro se intervenor in this docket. Mr. Howton objects to the
Commission’s approval of Applicants’ amended CCN before ERCOT or the Public Utility
Commission of Texas ("PUC") has identified where new energy will be generated or sourced.
The Applicants’ panel acknowledged that the 765-kV transmission line itself does not generate
real power. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:1-7.) If there is no confirmed generation of electrical
power, there is no need for the transmission lines, and the project constitutes a "Field of Dreams"
scenario. Mr. Howton further opposes approval of any route that uses Link F-20, including Route
894 and Route 487, because the record shows that Link F-20 would impose concentrated and
avoidable impacts on his land, the land of other affected property owners, his home, agricultural
operations, environmental resources, cultural resources, and the Cedar Valley/Buttermilk Creek
community. (Aaron Edward Howton Ex. 1; Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 115:1-24, 123:13-124:8.)
        Mr. Howton requests that the Administrative Law Judges recommend rejection of routes
utilizing Link F-20 and instead recommend PUC Staff witness John Poole’s second preferred
Route 296, or another route that avoids Link F-20 and better satisfies the statutory routing factors
under PURA § 37.056(c)(4). (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 91:21-92:4.) Mr. Poole also ranked Route
296 above Applicants Route 894 (Hearing Tr. Vol 4 at 92:4).
         When comparing Link F20 to Link F21 there were 25 Intervenors who filed testimony in
the PUC Interchange describing the impacts of a 765kV on Link F20 and only 5 Intervenors who
filed testimony concerning the impact on Link F21.
B. Applicants’ Failure to Explain Why Link F-20 Was Added or Selected over Link F-21
        During cross-examination, the record demonstrates that Applicants did not provide a
clear, fact-based explanation for why alternate Link F-20 was added after the public meeting.
Instead, Applicants’ routing witness gave general answers, referred back to prior RFI responses,
and characterized Link F-20 only as an alternative, without identifying any specific routing
constraint that required or justified the sharp 90-degree turn north through the Buttermilk Creek
and Cedar Valley area. During cross-examination, Mr. Howton stated that he had never built a
transmission line but had built many fences, and that a fence builder never makes a 90-degree
turn unless there is some constraint because of the additional cost, work, materials, and
maintenance. He asked Applicants’ witness to explain the reasoning when a direct route, Route
296, was available on Link F31 to F34 without 90-degree turns all the way to the Burnet County
line. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-121:17, 122:23-123:12.)
       Applicants acknowledged that Link F-20 introduces additional turning angles compared
with the more direct westward route. When questioned whether a line with six 90-degree turns
would generally cost more than a straighter route with fewer turns, Applicants’ witness admitted
that more turning angles generally increase cost. That admission supports the conclusion that
Link F-20 was not added because it was simpler, straighter, less expensive, or more efficient than
                                              Page 8
 the available westward alignment. Mr. Howton asked Applicants’ witness if there was some
constraint to continuing west, and Applicants’ witness answered no. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at
120:18-121:17, 123:9-12.)
        When asked who came up with the idea to add Link F-20, the routing witness first
described the decision as a team decision made after the public meeting and stated generally that
the link was added in consideration of comments regarding planned developments in the region.
In cross-examination of PUC Staff witness John Poole on June 10, 2026, Mr. Poole substantially
stated that parties are generally not supposed to consider future planned development when
routing transmission lines. When Applicants’ witness was pressed to identify the person
responsible for the idea, the witness ultimately stated that he was the person to ask. This
exchange shows that Applicants did not directly answer the question until further questioning
required the witness to accept responsibility for the routing decision. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at
121:18-122:22; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 117:23-118:8.)
        Most importantly, when asked why the route made the 90-degree turn north instead of
continuing west along a straighter path, the witness did not identify any specific engineering,
environmental, community, historical, cultural, cost, or land-use constraint that required the
addition of Link F-20. The witness instead stated that Link F-20 was merely an alternative to
other links in the area and not a substitution for the westward route. That response does not
explain why Link F-20 was added, why the 90-degree turn was selected, or why the route was
placed across the Buttermilk Creek area. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 122:23-123:12.)
        The testimony further confirms that there was no identified constraint preventing the
route from continuing west. When asked whether there were any constraints going west that
caused the decision to turn north, the witness answered no. That admission is significant. If there
was no constraint preventing the route from continuing west, then Applicants failed to provide a
credible basis for adding a more angled and more disruptive alternate link through the Buttermilk
Creek and Cedar Valley area. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 123:9-12.)
        The witness also admitted that he did not personally walk the ground along Link F-20
and did not speak with landowners along Link F-20 to obtain local information. Those
admissions matter because the Link F-20 area includes Buttermilk Creek, a significant
archaeological area, local cultural concerns, known artifact concerns, community values, and
landowner knowledge that may not appear on a desktop routing map. Applicant’s Appendix C,
Table 7-3 depicts Link F-20 as crossing 166 feet of open water springs and Link F-21 as crossing
0 feet of open water springs. Applicants added Link F-20 without obtaining meaningful site-
specific information from the people most familiar with the land. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 123:13-
124:8; Appendix C, Table 7-3.)
       Taken together, the cross-examination shows that Applicants did not give the
Administrative Law Judges a clear explanation for why Link F-20 was added. Applicants
admitted that additional turning angles generally increase cost, admitted there was no constraint
preventing the route from continuing west, admitted that the routing witness did not walk the
Link F-20 area, and admitted that he did not speak with affected landowners. Applicants’
explanation that Link F-20 was simply an alternative is not sufficient to justify placing a 765-kV
transmission line through an area with substantial community, cultural, historical, archaeological,
environmental, and landowner concerns. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8.)



                                              Page 9
 This is a failure of proof, not merely a disagreement about route preference. The Applicants had
the burden to provide a clear factual basis for selecting Link F-20 over less harmful alternatives,
and the record does not show that Link F-20 is reasonable, necessary, or superior under PURA §
37.056(c)(4).

       Applicants’ map in Figure 6-5 illustrates a distance of approximately 100 feet from Mr.
Howton’s Tract 5645 boundary to the centerline of Link F-20, and Applicants’ Table 7-5 lists
240 feet from his residence. That proximity is not a minor inconvenience. It demonstrates that
Link F-20 would place a 765-kV transmission line extremely close to Mr. Howton’s property
and residence, affecting the use, enjoyment, value, and safety concerns associated with the
property. (Applicants’ Fig. 6-5; Appendix F, Table 7-5; Aaron Edward Howton Exs. 2, 5, 9, 20.)
        Mr. Howton’s accepted testimony and exhibits describe the property as actively used
rural land, not vacant or speculative land. His exhibit index identifies evidence concerning Tract
5645, aerial views, farm and USDA documents, agricultural photographs, cattle, route maps, and
views from the residence. The ALJs should give substantial weight to the direct, localized
evidence of impact on an affected landowner. (Aaron Edward Howton Exs. 1-9, 18-20.)
C. Impact on Affected Landowners and Habitable Structures
        Applicants’ Environmental Assessment tables and habitable-structure materials
materially understate the residential impact of Link F-20. Applicants reported only two habitable
structures within 500 feet of the centerline on Link F-20 and one habitable structure within 500
feet on Link F-21. Those counts appear in Applicants’ Tables 7-2, 7-3, and 7-5 and related
Appendix F materials. Applicants also testified that the counts and measurements were based on
desktop mapping and aerial reconnaissance, not a ground or field survey. (Appendix F, Table 7-
5; Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 174:1-25, 197:9-20; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21.)
        That limitation matters. During cross-examination by Jason Howton, Intervenor (pro se)
Party No. 666, on June 10, 2026, Applicants’ witness Russell Marusak was questioned about a
residence near First Cedar Valley Baptist Church at 12551 FM 2843 on Tract 5649. Mr. Marusak
acknowledged that the identified house was inside the 500-foot distance for habitable structures
based on the graphic and that, if it met the standard for a habitable structure, Applicants would
adjust the Link F-20 count to three. The additional structure was identified at approximately 383
feet from the Link F-20 centerline. With that correction, Link F-20 has at least three habitable
structures within 500 feet of the centerline, at approximately 240 feet, 383 feet, and 405 feet,
while Link F-21 has only one listed habitable structure within 500 feet, at approximately 335
feet. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21; Appendix F, Table 7-5.)
        The corrected information also shows that Link F-20 places a heavier and more
concentrated burden on landowners. Link F-20 crosses or directly affects more separate tracts,
including Tracts 2811, 2812, 2817, 2821, 2823, 5644, 5646, 5649, and 5650, and borders
additional tracts including 5645 and 5651. By contrast, Link F-21 affects fewer tracts and only
one listed habitable structure within 500 feet. The F-20 structures also include homes occupied
by multiple family members, and the missed residence at the boundary of Tract 5649 is identified
in Bell County Tax Assessor records as owned by Bonney Trust and lived in by Carl Simpson.
(LCRA Interactive Map, BCEBH 765-kV CCN Filing; Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:3-11.)



                                             Page 10
        This dispute is material because prudent avoidance requires limiting exposure to electric
and magnetic fields at reasonable cost, and habitable structures are one of the most direct
measures of human impact. A route recommendation cannot be reliable if it is based on an
understated count of homes and an incomplete comparison between Link F-20 and Link F-21.
Correcting the F-20 count increases the direct-human-impact burden of Link F-20 and supports
reduced weight, correction, or re-evaluation of Route 894 and any route using Link F-20. 16 Tex.
Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B); Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 98:1-20.
D. Community Values and Cultural Resources
         Community values include more than population counts or map labels. In this case,
community values include the rural residential character of Cedar Valley in Salado, Texas,
agricultural use, family outdoor use, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, the archaeological
Buttermilk Creek drainage, and the community’s shared concern for historic and environmental
resources. During the cross-examination of Oncor witness Marusak by pro se Intervenor Party
No. 250, Mr. Howton asked why Applicants’ Environmental Data Evaluation, including Tables
7-2 and 7-3 concerning Link F-20, did not show First Cedar Valley Baptist Church as a cultural
resource located less than 1,000 feet from the proposed transmission-line centerline. Mr.
Marusak stated, "Yes, sir," when asked whether, if he was not disputing it, he was concurring
that it could be a cultural resource for Cedar Valley. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:1-7, 118:8-11.)
First Cedar Valley Baptist Church and the surrounding Buttermilk Creek community are relevant
to community values, historical and aesthetic values, and cultural-resource concerns under
PURA § 37.056(c)(4). A 765-kV transmission line near this community gathering place would
impose a permanent visual, cultural, and community burden.

        Mr. Marusak substantially stated that First Cedar Valley Baptist Church was not listed as
a cultural resource within 1,000 feet of the proposed 765-kV transmission line because
Applicants relied on historical markers and cultural-resource databases maintained by state
sources. Mr. Marusak did not dispute the church’s local or regional significance or age, and he
stated that if the structure is a historical marker, it should be in the table. Under PURA §
37.056(c)(4), a property can have cultural or historical significance even if it has never been
formally listed by the Texas Historical Commission. The church’s own history dates back to
1942, and it has served Cedar Valley continuously for more than 80 years, exceeding the 50-year
threshold commonly used by preservation agencies. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:8-119:8; First
Cedar Valley Baptist Church Direct Testimony at 1-7, PUC Interchange Item No. 3995.)
       First Cedar Valley Baptist Church is used for community meetings, Sunday worship,
funerals, weddings, disaster relief, youth programs, senior-citizen events, and holiday
celebrations. Cultural significance is not limited to listed buildings; it can also include cultural
landscapes and places associated with historical events. The absence of a formal Texas Historical
Commission designation does not establish the absence of cultural and historical significance.
Mr. Marusak stated that if the church is of cultural significance to the community, he did not
dispute that it is of cultural significance to a community. (First Cedar Valley Baptist Church
Direct Testimony at 1-7, PUC Interchange Item No. 3995; Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 118:22-119:8.)
         During Mr. Poole’s cross-examination by Dave Brown on June 10, 2026, Mr. Poole
substantially stated that schools and churches are important to avoid because those kinds of
facilities have many children and adults who come there. Yet Applicants did not give

                                             Page 11
 corresponding consideration in their Environmental Evaluation Data to First Cedar Valley
Baptist Church. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 148:13-149:6.)
        Recommending that a 765-kV transmission line be located within approximately 690 to
720 feet of First Cedar Valley Baptist Church does not satisfy prudent-avoidance or limited-
effects considerations. First Cedar Valley Baptist Church meets the standard for being
considered a cultural resource and should have been listed in the Environmental Data tables. It
also falls directly within PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A), community values, because it is a central
focus of the Cedar Valley community and served as a focal point for recovery after the April 12,
2022 tornado, when Governor Abbott pledged that the State of Texas would help Cedar Valley
and the church rebuild even better than before. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 115:15-119:8; Hearing Tr.
Vol. 4 at 54:24-55:3; Aaron Edward Howton Exs. 10-11.)
       The evidence supports a finding that Link F-20 would burden an established rural
community area in a way that Applicants did not fairly weigh. A routing decision that places
severe impacts on a small number of landowners and community features should not be
approved when a reasonable non-F-20 route, including Preferred Route 296, is available.
(Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 57:4-58:20, 91:21-92:4, 205:11-207:10.)
E. Endangered Species and Habitat
        During the SOAH Hearing on the Merits on June 10, 2026, Jason Howton, Intervenor
(pro se) Party No. 666, questioned Applicants’ panel witnesses during cross-examination about
endangered species and endangered-species habitat in the area of Link F-20. Mr. Marusak
confirmed that no site-specific field survey of Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat was conducted on
Link F-20, that the zero-acre ESA figure for Link F-20 reflected a GIS overlay of USFWS-
designated critical-habitat boundaries rather than a field survey, and that field environmental
surveys would occur after route selection. Mr. Marusak also confirmed that USFWS validation
caused Applicants to remove another link, while the record does not show comparable F-20-
specific USFWS validation before selection. (Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8.)
         That answer is significant because Intervenor Aaron Edward Howton, Party No. 250,
